newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan boosts president powers, streamlines state.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan boosts president powers, streamlines state.

text.p: Taiwan on Friday overcame deep divisions to change its constitution fundamentally, beefing up the president's powers at the expense of parliament and all but junking a largely redundant provincial government.
Champagne corks popped as the National Assembly speaker announced an overwhelming bipartisan consensus in a decisive final vote on a package of constitutional amendments.

Absent from the vote was the small New Party, whose members walked out to protest changes that they said gave the president too much power and risked provoking arch rival China, which has eyed the reform process with suspicion.

Deep differences between the ruling Nationalist Party and the leading opposition Democratic Progressive Party forced postponement until 1998 of a potentially explosive proposal to give Taiwan's people the right of plebiscite.
Still, Taiwan's mainstream parties hailed the breakthrough.
"These amendments are only a small step in the history of constitutional reform, but they are a major step in the history of Taiwan," said Democratic Progressive chairman Hsu Hsin-liang.
"The significance is immense," Hsu added. "For the first time, the will of the Taiwan people dominates the entire constitutional reforms."

The National Assembly has been largely eclipsed by the lawmaking Legislative Yuan, or parliament, but has been seated for the first time through popular elections, giving democratic input into its sole function -- amending the constitution.
"The reforms will benefit the entire nation and its people," Nationalist powerbroker Vincent Siew, who spearheaded the reform drive, told Reuters.
"They help us to achieve government re-engineering, allowing the government to be more efficient and more competitive."

The Nationalists put off an opposition push to legalise popular referendums, which scholars warned could undermine an uneasy status quo between Taiwan and communist China -- ideological rivals since their 1949 civil war split.

The package will marginalise the provincial government, a move that will save T$60 billion (US$2.2 billion) a year but which could kindle Beijing's suspicions that Taiwan is moving towards independence rather than eventual reunion with China.

The Republic of China, exiled on Taiwan since its 1949 loss of the mainland, has maintained a provincial authority distinct from the "national" government to bolster its increasingly untenable claim of being the legitimate ruler of "all China".
The government justified the phase-out on narrow grounds of efficiency, saying it would save T$60 billion (US$2.2 billion) a year and had nothing to do with independence from China.
Taipei, recognised by only 30 countries, has virtually abandoned its claim to sovereignty over the mainland and has tried to carve out a modicum of diplomatic "living space".

Defending its right to exist, Taiwan opposes China's demand that it reunify under communist rule but has not overtly sought to break away as a sovereign Republic of Taiwan -- a move that Beijing has vowed to crush by force of arms.

The amendments bolster the elected president's power by stripping the parliament, also elected, of the right to veto the president's nominee of cabinet chief and by granting the president the power to dissolve parliament.

Conversely, they give parliament the power to recall a president, but set a tough standard -- requiring a three-fifths vote of the full membership to impeach a chief executive and a two-thirds vote to sack him.

Despite warnings that Taiwan was creating a "super president" with vast powers unchecked by parliament, the main opposition supported the Nationalist-sponsored reform in hopes that its candidate will win the next presidential election.
